Systematic reviews

Cochrane Library Breast Enlargement Evidence

Cochrane systematic reviews and registered protocols relevant to breast enlargement and breast implants — wound drains, implant types, implants versus the patient's own tissue, mesh and fat transfer — summarised and linked to the original records on the Cochrane Library.

Home/Research library/Cochrane Library

This library collects every Cochrane systematic review and registered review protocol that bears on breast enlargement, breast implants and implant-based reconstruction — 3 completed reviews and 4 protocols registered with, or withdrawn by, Cochrane. Each entry links to the full record on cochranelibrary.com, with its DOI and PubMed citation where one exists, so the wording, dates and any later updates can be checked at source.

7Cochrane records
3Completed reviews
4Protocols
20 October 2026Compiled

What this library does and does not mean

Cochrane publishes independent systematic reviews that search for and appraise all available studies on a clinical question. A review here reports what the evidence showed when it was published; a protocol only states what a team intends to review — protocols contain no results, and one entry in this library was withdrawn before any review was written. Nothing here is a recommendation to have or avoid a procedure, and individual suitability always requires assessment by a qualified clinician.

Summaries and key points are condensed from the Cochrane abstracts and record pages for readability. They are not a substitute for the full reviews, which may have been updated since this library was compiled on 20 October 2026. Always read the current version on cochranelibrary.com.

Coverage

What the Cochrane evidence covers

The library is grouped into four areas, from the augmentation question itself to the reconstructive surgery evidence and the protocols still in progress.

Completed reviews

3 completed Cochrane Reviews: wound drains after breast surgery, different implant types, and implants versus autologous tissue flaps after mastectomy.

Augmentation directly

What the reviews say about breast augmentation itself — the drain trials, and why capsular-contracture research (implant insertion funnels) is still only a registered protocol.

Implant type evidence

Five small randomised trials (202 participants) comparing surfaces, fillers and shapes — and the review’s conclusion that implant choice cannot yet be based on randomised evidence.

Reconstruction evidence

Quality of life, satisfaction and complications with implants versus the patient’s own tissue across 35 non-randomised studies and 57,555 participants.

Protocols in progress

Registered protocols on insertion funnels, prepectoral mesh and acellular dermal matrices — what Cochrane is currently examining, with no results yet.

Evidence gaps

Where Cochrane has no review at all: cosmetic augmentation as a procedure, fat transfer for enlargement, breast uplift, fillers and non-surgical options.

All Cochrane records in this library

Grouped by topic. Each entry gives the record type, publication date, a short summary, the main findings or planned methods, and a direct link to the full record, DOI and PubMed citation.

Augmentation and implant technique

Cochrane records that address breast enlargement directly — wound drains after augmentation surgery and the implant insertion techniques used to prevent capsular contracture.

Wound drainage after plastic and reconstructive surgery of the breast

Cochrane Review · Published 21 October 2015

Whether surgical wound drains should be placed after breast augmentation, reduction or reconstruction. Three randomised trials (306 women, 505 breasts) were found out of 190 screened studies — all of them in breast reduction — comparing drains with no drains after surgery.

  • Across the three trials, drains produced no statistically significant improvement in infection, other wound complications, pain, bruising, seroma, haematoma or reoperation.
  • Women who were not drained left hospital a mean 0.77 days sooner (95% CI 0.40 to 1.14 days sooner; low-certainty evidence) — the only significant result.
  • No trials of drains after breast augmentation or breast reconstruction were identified, so the findings apply to breast reduction only.
  • Cochrane concludes that the limited evidence shows no significant benefit of routine post-operative drains, and that augmentation and reconstruction still require investigation.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD007258.pub3 · PMID 26487173

Breast implant insertion funnels for preventing capsular contracture

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 30 March 2026

Registered protocol for a review that will assess the effects of breast implant insertion funnels — devices used to guide the implant into place while minimising contact with skin — on capsular contracture rates in women having breast reconstruction or breast augmentation.

  • This is a protocol, not a completed review: no results are available yet.
  • The primary outcome planned is capsular contracture, alongside other complications, with both randomised and non-randomised studies eligible.
  • The protocol anticipates few, if any, randomised trials of funnels, because capsular contracture often appears years after surgery and has many causes.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD016344 · PMID 41909996

Implant types and materials

Cochrane reviews comparing implant surfaces, fillers and shapes, and what the randomised evidence does and does not establish about choosing between them.

Different types of implants for reconstructive breast surgery

Cochrane Review · Published 16 May 2016

Whether different breast implant types — textured or smooth, silicone or saline, anatomical or round, variable or fixed volume — change capsular contracture, complications, satisfaction and quality of life after reconstructive breast surgery. Five randomised trials with 202 participants were found.

  • Every comparison was rated very low quality evidence: the trials were small, at unclear or high risk of bias, and too different from each other to pool.
  • In one trial of 60 women, saline implants had less severe capsular contracture and higher satisfaction than silicone implants, but reinterventions were significantly more frequent with saline.
  • No comparison reached statistical significance for textured versus smooth silicone implants (1 study, 20 women) or anatomical versus round implants (1 study, 36 women).
  • No trials compared fifth-generation silicone implants or different manufacturers; the review concludes that surgeons still cannot counsel women on implant choice on the basis of randomised evidence.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD010895.pub2 · PMID 27182693

Implant-based reconstruction

Reviews and registered protocols on reconstruction after mastectomy: implants versus the patient's own tissue, and the meshes and dermal matrices used to support implants.

Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy

Cochrane Review · Published 31 October 2024

Implant-based versus own-tissue (flap) reconstruction after mastectomy — quality of life, satisfaction and short- and long-term complications. Thirty-five non-randomised studies with 57,555 participants met the criteria; no randomised trials were found.

  • Implants may reduce psychosocial well-being (mean difference -4.26 on a 0–100 scale; low-certainty evidence) and sexual well-being (-6.63; low-certainty) versus autologous flaps on BREAST-Q measures.
  • Women may be less satisfied with the reconstruction with implants (-5.96; low-certainty) and with the breast itself (-8.17; very low-certainty).
  • Long-term complications may be more frequent with implants (risk ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.22; very low-certainty), while implant surgery was about 125 minutes shorter (very low-certainty).
  • All evidence came from non-randomised studies (26 at serious overall risk of bias); the review found no superior technique for every woman and called for randomised trials.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD013821.pub2 · PMID 39479986

Mesh for immediate implant-based prepectoral breast reconstruction following mastectomy

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 17 June 2025

Registered protocol for a review of biological or synthetic mesh used to support a prepectoral implant (placed above the muscle) in immediate breast reconstruction after mastectomy.

  • This is a protocol, not a completed review: no results have been published.
  • It plans to compare mesh versus no mesh, and biological versus synthetic mesh, for complications, patient-reported outcomes and reoperation after prepectoral reconstruction.
  • Prepectoral placement is one of the placement options also discussed in breast augmentation, so the review will be relevant to implant positioning debate generally.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD015961 · PMID 40525534

Acellular dermal matrices for breast reconstruction surgery

Cochrane Protocol · Review in progress · Published 2015

Registered protocol for a review of acellular dermal matrices (biological meshes derived from human or animal skin) used around implants in immediate prosthetic breast reconstruction after cancer or risk-reducing surgery.

  • This protocol was registered in 2015; no completed review has been published under this title.
  • It plans to compare reconstruction with versus without acellular dermal matrix for seroma, infection, skin flap necrosis, haematoma, reconstruction failure and implant removal.
  • The protocol notes that some studies suggest dermal matrix may raise complication rates, which the review is intended to test.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD011966

Fat transfer

The Cochrane record on fat grafting — withdrawn before any review was completed — and the evidence gap it leaves.

Autologous fat grafting for breast reconstruction

Cochrane Protocol · Withdrawn · Published 29 June 2021

Protocol for a review of autologous fat grafting — transferring the patient's own fat into the breast — for breast reconstruction after cancer surgery. Cochrane withdrew the protocol because the authors were no longer able to complete the review.

  • Cochrane withdrew this protocol: "the authors are no longer able to complete this review", so no Cochrane systematic review of fat grafting exists under this title.
  • The protocol itself was published on 29 June 2021 and remains readable as a record of the intended methods.
  • No Cochrane review has examined fat transfer for cosmetic breast enlargement either.

Read the record on cochranelibrary.com → · DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD010793.pub2

Extracted data

Key findings from the Cochrane records

The statements below summarise what the Cochrane reviews found, and what the protocols and evidence gaps mean for breast enlargement. The right-hand column links to the source record.

Key findings from the Cochrane records
TopicWhat the Cochrane evidence showsSource
Wound drainsRandomised evidence does not support routine drains after breast surgery: in three trials (306 women) drains did not reduce complications, and hospital stay was about 0.8 days shorter without them. Every trial was in breast reduction — none in augmentation.Wound drainage after plastic and reconstructive surgery of the breast
Implant typeNo randomised trial of usable quality establishes one implant type as better than another. All five trials (202 participants) were rated very low quality evidence, and neither textured-versus-smooth nor anatomical-versus-round comparisons reached significance.Different types of implants for reconstructive breast surgery
Implants versus own tissueAcross 35 non-randomised studies (57,555 participants), implants may mean lower psychosocial and sexual well-being and less satisfaction than autologous flaps, but about 125 minutes shorter surgery — with low to very low certainty throughout.Implants versus autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction following mastectomy
Capsular contractureWhether implant insertion funnels reduce capsular contracture is being assessed in a review registered in 2026. No results exist yet, and the protocol expects few randomised trials to be found.Breast implant insertion funnels for preventing capsular contracture
Mesh and dermal matrixTwo registered protocols — mesh for prepectoral support and acellular dermal matrices — still have no completed review, leaving implant-support techniques without a Cochrane synthesis.Mesh for immediate implant-based prepectoral breast reconstruction following mastectomy
Fat transferCochrane has never published a review of fat transfer for breast enlargement. The protocol on fat grafting for reconstruction was withdrawn in 2021 because the authors could not complete it.Autologous fat grafting for breast reconstruction

Findings are paraphrased from Cochrane review abstracts (retrieved via PubMed, October 2026) and are stated with the certainty ratings Cochrane applied to them. Protocols report planned methods only. Verify each point against the linked record on cochranelibrary.com before relying on it.

Where the Cochrane evidence runs out

Cochrane has published no systematic review of cosmetic breast augmentation as a procedure — no review of augmentation techniques, implant placement planes, satisfaction after cosmetic surgery, or long-term outcomes in women who had implants for enlargement rather than reconstruction. The completed reviews here were written for breast reduction and post-mastectomy reconstruction; their findings are evidence about those settings, not direct evidence about augmentation for cosmetic purposes.

There is also no Cochrane review of fat transfer or autologous fat grafting for cosmetic breast enlargement (the reconstruction protocol was withdrawn in 2021), none of silicone gel implants used for cosmetic purposes, none of breast uplift (mastopexy), none of gynaecomastia surgery in men, and none of the non-surgical options discussed elsewhere on this site — fillers, platelet-rich plasma, threads or biostimulators. Absence of a Cochrane review does not mean a treatment works or does not work; it means the question has not been systematically synthesised at this level, and other evidence must be weighed instead.

Search the Cochrane Library yourself

Cochrane’s own search can be run directly: search the Cochrane Library for breast augmentation. Reviews carry identifiers of the form CD012345 (with .pubN suffixes for updated editions); the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) inside the Library also indexes thousands of individual trials on breast implants and breast surgery that no review has yet summarised.

Download and reuse

The structured dataset behind this page is available as JSON. It contains the record list, categories, summaries, key points and extracted findings, with DOI, PMID and source URLs.

Source and copyright

Cochrane reviews and protocols are published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in the Cochrane Library and remain the property of Cochrane and the respective authors, with abstracts distributed by PubMed. This library stores only our own summaries, paraphrased key points and links to the publicly available records; full abstracts and review texts are read on cochranelibrary.com.

For the wider published literature, see the PMC research library. For regulator guidance, see the FDA information library and the NHS information library. For academic patient education, see the Cleveland Clinic information library. For professional-society patient information on breast augmentation, see the ASPS information library.
